F ED ERA L EN ER GY RE GU LA TO RY CO M M IS S IO N | D O CK E T N O . RM 26 - 4 - 00 0




Execution Architecture for
Large-Load Interconnection
An expanded analysis of the DOE-identified principles and the Commission's June 2026 show
cause orders on the interconnection of large loads to the interstate transmission system



PREPARED BY

Abdur Rahman
Energy Sector Strategy and Operations Professional
Herndon, Virginia




July 2026
This report expands upon the author's public comment in Docket No. RM26-4-000, docketed as Accession No. 20260701-5236
and filed July 1, 2026.



The views expressed are the author's own and are offered in his individual capacity.
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N   A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




Executive Summary
On October 23, 2025, the Secretary of Energy directed the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, under
section 403 of the Department of Energy Organization Act, to consider an Advance Notice of Proposed
Rulemaking on the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads, generally those exceeding twenty
megawatts, to the interstate transmission system [1][2]. On June 18, 2026, the Commission converted that
inquiry into action, issuing tailored show cause orders under section 206 of the Federal Power Act to all six
regional grid operators under its jurisdiction and giving each sixty days to justify its existing tariff or file
reforms across five defined categories [3]. This report expands upon my public comment in the docket,
filed July 1, 2026 and docketed as Accession No. 20260701-5236 [8], into a fuller analysis of the DOE-
identified principles and of what the June orders now require in practice.

My central argument is unchanged from my filed comment, and the intervening Commission action has
strengthened it. The binding constraint on large-load interconnection reform is not policy intent. It is
execution design: the sequencing of interdependent legal, commercial, technical, and regulatory actions,
the assignment of ownership at each step, and the explicit allocation of costs and reliability responsibilities
across transitions. The country's reliability outlook makes the point unavoidable. The North American
Electric Reliability Corporation's 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment projects summer peak demand
growth of 224 gigawatts over the coming decade, a forecast that has quadrupled across three assessment
cycles, with thirteen of twenty-three assessment areas facing resource adequacy challenges [4]. Rules
written for that environment will be judged by whether they can be executed at pace, not by whether they
read well.

The analysis reaches four conclusions. A sixty-day expedited study target for flexible loads will hold only
if the process is rebuilt as a gated dependency sequence with named ownership and with curtailment
commitments treated as governed, auditable obligations. Full-cost responsibility will protect existing
customers only if the credit-back period is anchored to a measurable affordability standard and the interim
allocation of costs, before crediting completes, is specified in the rule itself. Reliability review of co-
location arrangements that involve partial plant shutdown must evaluate the transition sequence as such,
with completion of critical upgrades before load energization as the administrable default. And
implementation will succeed or fail on transition design: explicit treatment of pending requests and a
milestone-based runway. Section 8 translates these conclusions into execution priorities for the sixty-day
compliance filings the six grid operators now owe the Commission.


1. Introduction and Analytical Basis
I am an energy sector strategy and operations professional based in Herndon, Virginia. My work centers on
executing large-scale transformations in the U.S. power sector: the operational sequencing of separations
and restructurings among major energy companies, the transfer and continuity of supplier contracts and
regulatory obligations across complex multi-jurisdictional transitions, the commercialization of
technologies that reduce stress on the grid, and the design of utility cost-recovery approaches that reconcile
infrastructure investment with rate stability for existing customers. I write in my individual capacity, and
the views here are my own. This report elaborates on the comment I filed in Docket No. RM26-4-000 on
July 1, 2026 [8], and extends that comment to address the Commission's June 18, 2026 show cause orders,
which had not yet issued in final compliance posture when the docket record was first assembled.



FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                     Page 2
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N       A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




The report proceeds in four parts. Sections 2 and 3 establish the national context and the regulatory arc of
the docket. Sections 4 through 7 analyze each DOE-identified principle in turn, expanding the positions in
my filed comment with the design detail a workable rule will require. Section 8 sets out execution priorities
for the sixty-day compliance window the Commission has opened. Section 9 concludes.


2. The National Context: Demand Growth, Reliability Risk, and the Execution Gap
The demand environment into which any large-load rule will land is without precedent in the modern history
of the North American bulk power system. NERC's 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment, released in
January 2026, forecasts summer peak demand growth of 224 gigawatts over the 2026 to 2035 period, an
increase of more than sixty-nine percent over the 132 gigawatts projected only one year earlier, with winter
peak demand projected to grow by approximately 245 gigawatts over the same horizon [4]. The trajectory
of the forecast itself is the most telling fact. As Figure 1 shows, the ten-year growth projection has
quadrupled across three assessment cycles, from 55 gigawatts in the 2022 assessment to 224 gigawatts in
the 2025 assessment. Planning institutions built for incremental growth are now being asked to absorb step-
change growth, and NERC finds that thirteen of its twenty-three assessment areas face resource adequacy
challenges over the next ten years even as roughly 105 gigawatts of seasonal peak capacity remain slated
for retirement [4].




     Figure 1. Ten-year forecast of summer peak demand growth for the North American bulk power system, by Long-Term
           Reliability Assessment vintage. Data: NERC, 2025 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (January 2026) [4].

Large computing loads are the dominant driver. The Department of Energy's 2024 data center energy study,
prepared by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, found that data centers consumed about 4.4 percent
of total U.S. electricity in 2023, roughly 176 terawatt-hours, and projected consumption of between 325
and 580 terawatt-hours by 2028, equivalent to between 6.7 and 12 percent of forecast national consumption
[6]. Figure 2 summarizes that range. What matters for interconnection policy is not only the magnitude but
the character of this demand: it arrives in discrete, very large increments, on private development timelines
measured in quarters rather than the decade-scale horizons of transmission planning, and increasingly in
configurations, such as co-location with existing generation, that the current regulatory architecture was
never designed to study.




FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                         Page 3
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N            A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




     Figure 2. U.S. data center electricity consumption, actual (2014 and 2023) and projected scenario range (2028). Data:
     Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (December 2024) [6].

The institutional readiness picture reinforces the concern. NERC issued a Level 2 Alert on large load
interconnection, study, commissioning, and operations in September 2025, and its March 2026 white paper
on emerging large loads concluded that existing Reliability Standards and interconnection requirements do
not adequately mitigate the reliability risks these loads introduce, in part because neither large loads nor the
entities serving them are registered functions under the current reliability framework [5]. NERC's own
comments in this docket, filed in November 2025, pressed for consistent visibility into new large loads,
clear coordination requirements among entities, and robust planning processes [5]. In plain terms, the
mandatory-standards architecture does not yet reach the problem, which means near-term protection must
come from tariff design, and tariff design is exactly what this docket and the June 2026 orders now govern.

Federal policy has moved on the supply side in parallel. Executive Order 14156 declared a national energy
emergency in January 2025, and Presidential Determination No. 2026-10, issued April 20, 2026 under
section 303 of the Defense Production Act, designated grid infrastructure, equipment, and supply chain
capacity, including transformers, high-voltage components, and power electronics, as essential to the
national defense and authorized the Department of Energy to accelerate domestic production [7]. That
determination addresses the equipment side of the constraint. This docket addresses the process side. Both
share a diagnosis I have observed repeatedly in large energy programs: the limiting factor is rarely the
absence of capital or intent, and very often the absence of a disciplined sequence. Equipment with multi-
year lead times, studies with contested queues, curtailment commitments that must be verifiable under
stress, and phased energizations that must not outrun their compensating upgrades are all, at bottom,
sequencing problems. A rule that does not govern the sequence will not deliver the outcome.


3. The Regulatory Arc of Docket No. RM26-4-000
The docket originated with the Secretary of Energy's October 23, 2025 proposal under section 403 of the
Department of Energy Organization Act, which directed the Commission to consider an Advance Notice
of Proposed Rulemaking on reforms to how large loads, generally those with demand above twenty
megawatts, interconnect to the interstate transmission system [1]. The ANOPR sought input on four DOE-



FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                              Page 4
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N                 A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




identified principles: whether flexible and curtailable loads should move through interconnection studies
faster, and whether such studies could be completed within sixty days; whether large loads should bear the
full cost of the grid upgrades their interconnection requires, with those costs credited back over time; how
reliability should be evaluated when an existing plant partially shuts down to serve a co-located customer,
including whether required upgrades must be completed first; and how any changes should be implemented,
including the treatment of requests already under review [2]. The Commission subsequently extended the
comment period, and the record grew substantially; Commission staff reviewed more than 3,500 pages of
public comments in developing the actions that followed [3]. My own comment, organized around the same
four principles, was docketed on July 1, 2026 [8].

On June 18, 2026, the Commission acted. Rather than proceeding first to a generic proposed rule, it issued
tailored show cause orders under section 206 of the Federal Power Act to each of the six regional
transmission organizations and independent system operators under its jurisdiction: PJM, MISO, SPP,
CAISO, ISO-NE, and NYISO, in Docket Nos. EL26-67-000 through EL26-72-000 [3]. Each grid operator
and its transmission owners have sixty days to either justify why their current tariffs remain just and
reasonable without provisions tailored to large loads, or to file tariff changes addressing five categories of
reform: efficient transmission service application and study processes, including consideration of
alternative transmission technologies; prevention of cost shifting together with transparency into
transmission costs; accommodation of co-location arrangements and behind-the-meter generation; new
transmission services for flexible large loads; and a defined process for studying generating facilities that
serve electrically proximate and co-located loads [3]. Separately, each operator must file, within thirty days,
an informational report describing how it intends to ensure adequate generation for existing and new large
loads [3]. The orders build on earlier regional actions, including a December 2025 order directing PJM to
adopt transparent tariff rules for co-located loads and the Commission's approval of SPP's High Impact
Large Load study framework [3].

The structural significance of the June orders is easy to miss. The Commission has moved the question
from whether reform is warranted to how each region will operationalize it, on a defined clock, with the
burden resting on the grid operators. That is a shift from policy formation to execution, and it makes the
execution-layer considerations in my filed comment the near-term deliverable rather than a background
concern. Table 1 maps the four DOE-identified principles to the five reform categories in the show cause

4. Expedited Interconnection for Flexible and Curtailable Loads
Flexibility should be rewarded with speed. A load that can verifiably curtail during system stress imposes
materially less risk than an inflexible load of the same size, and it can be integrated with a smaller reliability
buffer and a lighter firm-upgrade obligation. The process should recognize that difference directly, and the
June orders now instruct every region to consider both efficient study processes and new service categories
for flexible large loads [3]. On the threshold question the ANOPR posed, my answer is yes: an expedited
pathway for genuinely flexible loads is sound policy, and a sixty-day study is achievable. But it is
achievable only under conditions that most current intake processes do not satisfy, and a sixty-day window
laid on top of an unsequenced process will miss.

The reason compressed timelines fail is rarely the study itself. It is that the actions surrounding the study,
data acquisition and validation, contractual commitments, system-configuration decisions, and regulatory
confirmations, are performed in parallel and out of order, so a late-surfacing dependency forces rework that
consumes the time the compressed schedule was meant to save. Figure 3 contrasts the two designs. In the
unsequenced version, the study launches at intake while its own prerequisites are still unsettled; when a
dependency surfaces at day thirty-six, the rework runs well past the target. In the sequenced version, the
sixty days are divided into gates: prerequisite inputs are confirmed before the study begins, the study
executes against a frozen input set, dependent commitments and configuration decisions follow the study's
outputs, and regulatory confirmation closes the window. The critical path is explicit from day one rather
than discovered at day forty.




   Figure 3. Two intake designs for a sixty-day expedited interconnection study. Illustrative schematic prepared by the author.




FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                                    Page 6
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N   A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




If the Commission and the regions proceed, the expedited pathway should carry three requirements. First,
a complete-application standard: a defined set of inputs, load characteristics, curtailment capability,
telemetry provisions, and site electrical data, that must be confirmed before the sixty-day clock starts, so
the study never runs against a moving target. Second, a published dependency sequence specifying which
inputs gate the study and which downstream actions depend on its outputs, with named ownership at each
step across the transmission provider, the interconnecting customer, and any co-located generator, so no
required action falls into the gaps between organizations. Third, and most important, the curtailment
commitment that earns the expedited treatment must itself be a governed, auditable obligation: defined
triggers, verification through telemetry, audit rights, and stated consequences for non-performance. The
entire reliability case for faster interconnection rests on that commitment being executable when the system
needs it, and a general assurance is not an executable commitment.

There is precedent for this discipline on the generation side. Order No. 2023 restructured generator
interconnection around readiness requirements, clustered studies, and firm deadlines precisely because
open-ended, serially processed queues had failed under volume [9]. The load side now faces the same
volume problem with less institutional scaffolding, and NERC's gap assessment confirms that no
mandatory-standards backstop yet exists for large-load behavior [5]. The tariff, in other words, must carry
the full weight of the governance. Without the three requirements above, a sixty-day target becomes either
aspirational, missed in practice and eroding confidence in the reform, or nominal, met on paper while
unresolved dependencies surface after energization, which is exactly where reliability exposure is highest.


5. Full-Cost Responsibility and Credit-Back Design
Large loads should bear the full incremental cost of the upgrades their interconnection requires. Socializing
those costs across the existing ratepayer base would let new high-intensity loads shift their own
infrastructure burden onto residential and commercial customers who gain nothing from the
interconnection, at a time when affordability pressure on those customers is already severe. The cost-
causation logic is straightforward: upgrades that would not have been needed but for the new
interconnection should be paid for by the party that caused them. Full-cost responsibility for the
interconnecting load is the correct default, and the June orders' cost-shifting and transparency category
confirms that the Commission views ratepayer protection as a co-equal objective with speed [3].

The harder question is the credit-back design, because that design decides whether full-cost recovery
actually protects existing customers or merely defers the same cost migration. Two points. First, the credit-
back period should be anchored to a measurable affordability standard for existing customers, not set as a
fixed default term chosen for administrative convenience. If crediting returns costs to the large load on a
schedule calibrated to hold the upgrade-attributable rate impact on existing customers at or below a defined
threshold, the mechanism does its job. A uniform arbitrary period will either over-credit the large load,
which is a subsidy, or under-protect existing customers during the interval before crediting takes hold.
Tying the period to an explicit anchor makes the distributional effect deliberate instead of incidental.
Second, the rule should state how upgrade costs are allocated between the new load and the existing
customer base during the transition, before crediting is complete. The interval between energizing an
upgrade and fully offsetting it through credit-back is where cost migration to existing ratepayers happens
unnoticed, and Figure 4 illustrates the difference between a design that manages that interval and one that
leaves it to chance.

  Figure 4. Existing-customer rate exposure under an uncalibrated fixed-term credit-back and under an affordability-anchored

The transparency requirement in the June orders is the natural enforcement companion to this design. An
affordability anchor is only meaningful if the upgrade-attributable rate impact can be observed, which
requires that interconnection-driven transmission costs be identified and reported rather than absorbed into
undifferentiated rate base. Cost allocation between new loads and existing ratepayers should be a designed
result, stated in the tariff and measurable against a defined affordability objective, not a residual that falls
out of formulas whose distributional effects were never made explicit. Regions that specify the interim
allocation and the anchor in their compliance filings will produce more consistent and more defensible
outcomes than those that leave both to case-by-case resolution, and they will spare themselves years of
contested proceedings over cost responsibility that the tariff could have settled at the outset.


6. Reliability Review Where Generation Is Reconfigured to Serve Co-Located Load
The co-location scenario the ANOPR describes, an existing power plant partially shutting down its grid
deliveries to serve a new large customer at the same site, deserves particular scrutiny because it stacks two
reliability transitions into one event: generation is reconfigured while a very large new load comes online
at the same location. Reliability review here must evaluate phased execution risk, not just steady-state
resource adequacy. A co-location arrangement can be perfectly adequate once fully established and still
open a serious reliability gap during the transition, when the plant's output to the grid is reduced before, or
faster than, the compensating upgrades and the load's own flexibility measures are in place. Figure 5 makes
the exposure visible: in the unsequenced case, grid support is withdrawn months before the offsetting
measures are operational, and the shaded interval is precisely the window in which a system contingency
finds the region short.




FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                             Page 8
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N             A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




    Figure 5. Reliability exposure in a partial-shutdown co-location transition under two sequencing approaches. Illustrative
                                                 schematic prepared by the author.

The Commission should therefore treat the transition sequence itself as a subject of reliability review. The
evaluation should fix the order in which the partial shutdown, the load energization, and any required
upgrades occur relative to one another, and it should confirm that no interval exists in which grid support
has been withdrawn but the offsetting measures are not yet operational. On the Commission's specific
question whether required upgrades must be completed first, the answer should generally be yes.
Completing critical upgrades before energizing the load is a reasonable, administrable safeguard that
converts an ambiguous timing risk into a defined precondition, and it is far easier to verify than a
probabilistic assurance about interim operating procedures. The June orders' fifth reform category, a defined
process for studying generating facilities that serve electrically proximate and co-located loads, is the right
vehicle: the study process the regions file should require a transition sequence plan as part of the application,
with the sequence enforceable through the interconnection agreement rather than left as a planning
assumption [3].

On future load growth, the Commission should fold reasonably foreseeable expansion at the site into the
initial evaluation. Large-load sites, and data center campuses especially, expand in phases, and an
assessment scoped only to the first phase understates the eventual demand on reconfigured generation and
transmission. Evaluating against a credible growth trajectory at the outset reduces repeated interconnection
review and the reliability uncertainty that accompanies each expansion. One further institutional point
belongs here. Because NERC's gap assessment finds that large loads sit outside the registered-entity
framework and that existing Reliability Standards do not adequately address their behavior [5], the co-
location study process and the interconnection agreement are, for now, the only binding instruments
available to govern transition risk. The regions should draft them with that weight in mind, specifying
verification responsibilities and operating obligations that a mandatory standard would otherwise carry.




FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                                Page 9

7. Implementation and the Treatment of Pending Requests
Implementation is itself an execution problem, and the transition between regimes is where avoidable
disruption concentrates. The Commission and the regions should publish an explicit treatment for in-flight
requests rather than leaving transition questions to individual resolution, which breeds inconsistency and
disputes. A clear rule specifying which requirements attach to requests at defined stages of review as of the
effective date, together with a defined path for pending requests either to continue under prior terms or to
opt into the new framework, will cut uncertainty and prevent a backlog of contested transition calls.
Interconnection customers make siting and capital decisions on the strength of the regime they applied
under; a transition rule that is knowable in advance is worth more to investment certainty than any single
substantive reform.

The June orders make this immediate rather than hypothetical. Whatever tariff changes each region files
must arrive with transition mechanics attached: the treatment of every request already in its queue, the
effective-date logic, and a short, defined implementation runway with milestones, so transmission
providers, interconnecting customers, and co-located generators can align their processes before the
requirements bind. The thirty-day informational reports on generation adequacy should be built the same
way. A static reserve-margin statement will satisfy the letter of the obligation and inform no one. A useful
report is a dependency inventory: the expected energization schedule of large loads in the region set against
the confirmed commercial operation dates of the resources intended to serve them, with the gaps, and the
owner of each gap, identified. Reforms of this scope succeed or fail largely on transition design, and a
milestone-based plan is the most reliable way to capture the intended benefits without creating a new source
of delay.


8. From Principles to Compliance: Execution Priorities for the Sixty-Day Window
The show cause orders place six regional institutions, each with its own market design, stakeholder
structure, and starting tariff, on the same sixty-day clock. The Commission was explicit that a one-size-fits-
all solution is not the current most efficient path, and the substantive answers will rightly differ by region
[3]. The execution disciplines, however, should not differ, because the failure modes they prevent are
universal. Drawing on the frameworks described in Section 1, I would evaluate any compliance filing, and
I would encourage the Commission to evaluate them, against five disciplines: dependency sequencing,
named ownership, governed curtailment obligations, affordability anchoring, and transition governance.

Two observations about how these disciplines interact. The first is that they are mutually reinforcing rather
than separable. A gated study sequence without named ownership stalls at the gates; a curtailment
obligation without verification collapses the reliability case for the expedited pathway it enabled; an
affordability anchor without cost transparency cannot be measured; and a well-designed regime without
transition governance spends its first two years in litigation over which requests it covers. Regions that file
on four of the five will discover the fifth in the compliance docket. The second observation is that the
informational report and the tariff filing should be drafted as one exercise. The thirty-day adequacy report,
done as a dependency inventory, will surface exactly the sequencing constraints, generation timing against
load energization, that the tariff's study process and co-location provisions must then govern. Treating the
two filings as unrelated deliverables wastes the only structured look at the region's real critical path that
this proceeding will produce.

A final word on what the Commission should expect to receive. The temptation in a justify-or-reform
posture is to file the justification: a defense of the existing tariff supplemented by commitments to study
the harder questions. In a demand environment where the ten-year forecast has quadrupled in three cycles
and the standards framework does not yet reach the loads in question, that posture defers exactly the design
work the moment requires. The regions that treat the sixty days as an execution-design exercise, and file
tariffs that specify sequences, owners, verification, anchors, and transitions, will not only satisfy the orders.
They will hold the durable advantage in attracting the very loads this proceeding is about, because
sophisticated large customers site where the path to power is credible, and credibility in this domain is a
published, governed sequence.


9. Conclusion
The Commission is addressing a real and pressing national problem: enabling the interstate transmission
system to absorb rapid large-load growth in a way that is timely, orderly, reliable, and fair to existing
customers. The record now spans a Secretarial directive, an Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking,
thousands of pages of public comment, and six tailored show cause orders that convert principle into
obligation on a sixty-day clock. Whatever each region files, and whatever rule the Commission ultimately
adopts, will depend as much on execution design, sequencing interdependent actions, assigning clear
ownership, governing flexibility commitments, and allocating costs and reliability responsibilities explicitly
across transitions, as on the substantive policy choices themselves. I urged the Commission in my filed


FERC Docket No. RM26-4-000                                                                                                    Page 11
 E X E C U T IO N ARC H I T EC T UR E F OR LA R GE - L O A D I N T ER C ON N EC T I O N   A . R AH M A N | J U L Y 2026




comment to build these execution-layer considerations into any rule it proposes [8]. The June orders have
now made that layer the immediate work of the industry, and this report is offered as a contribution to doing
that work well.


About the Author
Abdur Rahman is an energy sector strategy and operations professional based in Herndon, Virginia. Trained
as a mechanical engineer, he spent five years in oil and gas field engineering operations before moving into
strategy consulting focused on large-scale transformation in the U.S. energy sector, where his work has
included operational leadership on one of the largest corporate separations in the sector's history. He holds
a Master of Business Administration.
